name: Programming languages
summary: What actually separates one language from another in practice: how the code runs, when types are checked, who frees memory, and which styles of program and concurrency it makes easy.
howItWorks: Syntax is the visible difference, but a few deeper choices decide how a language behaves in production. The first is how the code runs. C, C++, Rust, Go, Zig and Haskell (with GHC) are compiled ahead of time to machine code for one operating system and CPU. Java, Scala and Clojure compile to bytecode for the JVM, C# and F# to intermediate language for .NET, Erlang and Elixir to bytecode for BEAM; a runtime virtual machine then compiles the busy parts to machine code as the program runs. Python’s main implementation, CPython, compiles source to bytecode too, but runs it in an interpreter loop. The second is typing. A statically typed language (Java, C#, Go, Rust, Haskell) checks types at compile time, and many infer them, so `let x = 5;` in Rust needs no annotation. A dynamically typed language (Python, Clojure, Erlang, Elixir, Racket) attaches types to values and checks them as each line runs. Strong and weak are looser words for how willingly a language converts between types on its own: JavaScript turns `"1" + 1` into `"11"`, Python raises a `TypeError`. The third is memory. In C and Zig the programmer frees what they allocate. Java, Go, Python and most others use a garbage collector. Rust checks ownership rules at compile time and frees each value when its owner goes out of scope, with no collector. The rest is style and concurrency: which paradigms the language favours (object-oriented, functional) and how it runs many things at once (OS threads, `async`/`await`, goroutines, lightweight processes).
analogy: Ways of getting dinner from a recipe. A compiled language is a meal cooked ahead and frozen: quick to serve, but only in kitchens with the right oven. A language on a virtual machine ships a meal kit that any kitchen with the standard equipment finishes on site, and the cook gets faster at the dishes ordered most. An interpreted language sends the cook along to read the recipe out, step by step, every time.
useWhen: Choosing a language for a new service: match its runtime, typing and memory model to the job, not just its syntax
Explaining why the same algorithm is fast in one language and slow in another, or why one crashes on a type error only in production
Picking between a garbage collector (simpler code, some pauses) and manual or ownership-based memory (predictable, more work)
Mixing languages: languages that share a runtime (JVM, .NET, BEAM) can call each other’s libraries directly
avoidWhen: Ranking languages as fast or slow in general: the implementation, the libraries and the workload matter more than the language’s name
Treating “compiled” and “interpreted” as fixed labels: CPython compiles to bytecode, and JIT compilers turn VM bytecode into machine code
Choosing on paradigm alone: most modern languages mix object-oriented and functional features
example: A chat server keeps 100,000 connections open, each mostly waiting. In Erlang or Elixir each connection gets its own BEAM process, which starts at 327 words (2,616 bytes on a 64-bit machine), about 262 MB for all of them, and the runtime switches out any process after 4,000 reductions, roughly function calls, so none can hog a core. In Go each connection gets a goroutine whose stack starts at a few kilobytes and grows only when needed. In Java 21 each can get a virtual thread instead of an OS thread. C and Rust have no such scheduler built into the language, so the usual design there is an event loop in which a few OS threads serve every connection. Same job, four concurrency models, each a consequence of how the language and its runtime were designed.

print(add(1, 2))        # 3: dynamic typing, + on two ints
print(add("1", "2"))    # 12: the same code on two strings
add("1", 2)          # strong typing: no silent conversion

sections.title: Typing: static or dynamic, strong or weak, inferred
body: Static and dynamic answer when types are checked. Rust is statically typed, so the compiler must know the type of every variable before the program runs, and C# says every variable “has a type known at compile time.” Python checks as it goes: a name can hold an `int` now and a `str` later, and annotations are optional, because “the Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations.” Gradual typing sits in between: Elixir is adding set-theoretic types to its compiler, with a `dynamic()` type for values checked at run time.

Inference removes most of the cost of static types. Haskell, F#, Scala and Rust work out the types of local values from how they’re used, so the code reads almost like a dynamic language while the compiler still checks it.

Strong and weak have no agreed definition. They usually mean how far the language converts values between types on its own. JavaScript’s `+` converts the other operand to a string if either side is a string, so `"1" + 1` is `"11"`. Python refuses the same expression with a `TypeError`, and Java’s specification calls the language “strongly and statically typed.”

sections.title: Memory: manual, garbage collected or owned
body: In C, memory from `malloc` stays allocated until the program passes it to `free`; forgetting leaks it, and freeing the same block twice is undefined behaviour. Zig keeps that model on purpose: the language “performs no memory management on behalf of the programmer,” and every function that allocates takes an allocator as a parameter, which is why Zig needs no runtime and suits kernels and embedded devices. C++ is manual too, but destructors release resources when an object goes out of scope (RAII), which Stroustrup describes as memory management that is “safe and implicit without a garbage collector.”

Most languages hand memory to a garbage collector instead. Java’s specification puts it bluntly: objects “are never explicitly deallocated.” CPython frees most objects as soon as their reference count drops to zero and runs a cycle collector for the rest. BEAM gives every process its own small heap and collects each one separately.

Rust takes a third route. Every value has one owner, the compiler checks the ownership rules, and the value is freed when its owner goes out of scope. There is no collector and, in the Rust book’s words, none of these checks slow the program down while it runs; the cost is learning the rules.

sections.title: Paradigms and concurrency
body: Paradigm is about how a program is organised. Object-oriented languages bundle data with the methods that act on it; functional languages build programs from functions and immutable values. Few languages are pure examples: C# describes itself as object-oriented with features from other paradigms, Scala and F# mix both, and Clojure calls itself a functional language with a dynamic emphasis.

Concurrency is often where languages differ most. Go multiplexes cheap goroutines onto OS threads; Erlang and Elixir run millions of isolated processes that share nothing and exchange copied messages; Java 21 added virtual threads; C# offers `async`/`await` over Tasks. The models are compared in Synchronous and asynchronous execution.

kinds.name: Compiled to machine code
kinds.summary: A compiler turns the whole program into machine code for one operating system and CPU before it runs, so it starts fast and needs no virtual machine.
body: C, C++, Rust, Zig, Go and Haskell (with GHC) are compiled ahead of time. The output is an executable for one target, such as Linux on x86-64; running it elsewhere means compiling again. There is no warm-up and no interpreter, so start-up is quick, and nothing extra has to be installed on the machine that runs it.

Native doesn’t mean there’s no runtime. Go statically links its runtime, garbage collector included, into every binary, and GHC’s runtime system collects garbage too. C, C++, Rust and Zig ship no collector at all. The line also blurs from the other side: Racket CS compiles Racket to machine code through Chez Scheme, while the older Racket BC compiled to bytecode and finished the job with a JIT.

kinds.name: Run on a virtual machine
kinds.summary: The compiler emits portable bytecode for a runtime such as the JVM, .NET or BEAM, which loads it, compiles the busy parts to machine code and manages memory and threads.
body: Java, Scala and Clojure compile to JVM class files; C# and F# to Common Intermediate Language for .NET; Erlang and Elixir to `.beam` files for BEAM. One build runs on every platform the runtime supports, and the runtime supplies the garbage collector, threads or processes, and the standard library. Languages on the same runtime share libraries: Scala imports Java classes directly, and a class written in one .NET language can be subclassed in another.

The cost is the runtime itself: it has to be installed or bundled, it takes time to start, and code runs slower until the JIT has compiled the hot paths. Ahead-of-time options such as GraalVM Native Image and .NET Native AOT trade some dynamic features for a single native executable. See Runtime virtual machines for how the JVM, CLR and BEAM differ.

kinds.name: Interpreted
kinds.summary: An interpreter reads the program and carries it out as it goes, with no separate build step, at the cost of speed in tight loops.
body: Pure interpreters that re-read source text are rare now. CPython, the standard Python, compiles each module to bytecode first and then runs that bytecode in an interpreter loop, one instruction at a time, without turning it into machine code. There is no build step to wait for, but a tight loop sends every instruction through the interpreter, and checks every type, on every pass.

The difference from a VM-hosted language is mostly what happens to hot code. The JVM and .NET compile it to machine code; CPython, by default, doesn’t. Python 3.13 added an experimental JIT compiler, disabled by default, so even this line is moving.

story: For the first decades, the main question was how close to the machine to sit. Dennis Ritchie built C at Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973, with its most creative period in 1972, as a systems language for the young Unix; it grew out of the typeless BCPL and B and gave them a type structure. Bjarne Stroustrup started “C with Classes” down the corridor in 1979, and the first commercial C++ came out in October 1985. Both compiled straight to machine code and left memory to the programmer.

Others traded speed for convenience or safety. Guido van Rossum started Python over the 1989 Christmas holidays at CWI, building on his work on the interpreted language ABC, and posted it to Usenet in February 1991. A committee formed in 1987 to unify more than a dozen lazy functional languages published Haskell 1.0 on 1 April 1990. Java (1996) and C# (2002) made compiling to a portable virtual machine with a garbage collector the default for business software.

The 2000s and 2010s brought languages built for specific pains. At Google, Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson started Go on 21 September 2007 because they had to choose between efficient compilation, efficient execution and ease of programming; Go aimed for all three, with garbage collection and concurrency built in. Graydon Hoare began Rust in 2006, Mozilla sponsored it from 2009, and Rust 1.0 arrived in May 2015 with memory safety enforced by the compiler instead of a collector.

choices.choice: Compile to the machine, or to a portable virtual machine
choices.why: Native code starts fast and needs nothing installed, but has to be rebuilt for every platform. Java targeted networked devices where code had to run on any client, so it compiled to bytecode and let the runtime finish the job.

choices.choice: Check types before the program runs, or while it runs
choices.why: Static checking catches mistakes early and lets the compiler optimise; dynamic typing is quicker to write and change. Go’s designers set out to combine the ease of an interpreted, dynamically typed language with the efficiency and safety of a statically typed, compiled one.

choices.choice: Collect garbage, or prove memory safety at compile time
choices.why: Garbage collection removed whole classes of memory bugs but cost run time and memory. Rust’s ownership rules give the same safety with checks done entirely by the compiler, at the price of a steeper learning curve.

choices.choice: Keep the language small and leave memory to the programmer
choices.why: Zig has no runtime and no hidden allocations, so the same code works in kernels, embedded devices and real-time software where a collector or hidden control flow isn’t acceptable.
